mappings.note: The LED lights only one way round because current passes through it in one direction only: effect tied to cause. Not LO-18, because the LED is not being compared with another device here.
The switch completes or breaks the circuit, which is an explanation of how current is controlled. Not LO-17, because a role in the circuit rather than an observable feature is asked for.

The home-made switch is ON when the safety pin bridges both drawing pins and closes the gap: the condition for current to flow. Not LO-27, which covered building the switch rather than explaining its states.
Names the open-circuit state produced by an OFF switch, part of explaining when current does and does not flow.
Sorts true from false statements about where a switch may sit and when a lamp glows; all three statements are about how the circuit behaves, so LO-22.

The longer line of the cell symbol is a circuit-diagram convention, and LO-25 names electric circuits among the diagrams to be handled. Not LO-17, because a symbol, not the physical cell, is in question.
The shorter thicker line as the negative terminal: the companion symbol convention.
The crossed circle as the lamp symbol, again diagram vocabulary rather than a property of the lamp.
How a closed switch is drawn. Diagram convention, so LO-25 rather than LO-22, where the switch's effect on the circuit is the point.
Defines circuit diagram as the symbol drawing of a circuit.
Why symbols beat realistic pictures: quicker to draw and understood everywhere. Still about the practice of drawing circuit diagrams, so LO-25 rather than CG-SCI1.
Names the conductor class for materials current passes through easily. Not LO-18, because a category is named rather than two materials told apart.
Names the insulator class, the companion category-naming item.
How the conduction tester shows that an object conducts, i.e. how the test reads out. That is the investigation outcome, not the sorting of materials that follows.
Picks the plastic scale out of three metal objects as the one that leaves the lamp dark: differentiating conductors from insulators, the example named in LO-18.
Metal, specifically copper, for wires, chosen against rubber, plastic and glass. A property-based discrimination, so LO-18, not LO-29, where the everyday consequence would be the point.
Plastic and rubber sleeving to prevent shocks is the insulator idea used in daily life for safety. Not LO-18, because the material is given and the reason for the everyday practice is what is asked.

Both assertion and reason concern the conductor and insulator split, with the twist that the reason does not explain the assertion. The subject knowledge tested is LO-18; the logical form alone does not move it to CG-SCI1.
The body conducts because of the water and salts in it, so the answer is the cause behind the hazard. Not LO-29, because the item stops at the reason and does not ask for a safety practice.

Direct and alternating current distinguished by where each comes from. LO-18 is not available for this, since it covers materials and organisms, so the explanation-of-phenomena outcome is the honest home.
Ranks silver above copper among conductors, which is discriminating materials by how well they conduct. Not LO-19, because the item does not place a material into a class but grades within one.
Again the false claim that a switch is the source of current; the item rests on knowing what drives and what controls the current in a circuit.
Rubber band against copper, iron and graphite: the insulator is picked out from three conductors. Note that graphite as a conducting non-metal is what makes this harder than the plastic-scale item.
A broken filament in a series pair stops both lamps because the single path opens: effect traced to cause.
Insulation left on the wire ends keeps the circuit open, so the lamp stays dark. The insulator fact is the premise; the item asks for the consequence, which is LO-21.
Which symbols belong in a torch circuit diagram: battery, switch, lamp and wires. Diagram composition, so LO-25.
Reads one switch combination off the circuit and says which lamp lights, relating the state of each branch to the result.
The both-switches-ON case of the same circuit. Shares LO-21 with its sibling because the two items differ only in the switch states, not in the skill.

Rules out the switch being ON as a cause of a dead circuit, which requires matching each candidate fault to its effect. Not LO-20, because no test is planned, unlike the list-the-reasons-and-investigate item earlier in the chapter.
Picks the two figures where cells are wired positive to positive and so nothing flows: failure traced to the arrangement.
Choosing the LED-of-known-polarity method to find an unmarked cell's terminals is designing a workable test. Not LO-17, because the markings that identification relies on are unreadable.
What apparatus is needed and what procedure to follow to find which of six cells still work: an investigation specified end to end.

Correct answer wires cell one's positive to cell two's negative and then respects the LED's polarity, so the item turns on the connection rules that make the circuit work. Not LO-25, since no diagram is drawn.

Which everyday activity fails during a two-day power cut, distinguishing mains-dependent from battery-powered and non-electrical ones. Day-to-day application, not LO-19, because the sorting is of activities rather than materials.

The solar panel as the source in the toy-fan project is part of building a working circuit from available parts, which is LO-27. Not LO-29, because the context is a construction project rather than daily life.
Button cells named from their small flat round shape and their use in watches and hearing aids: identification by appearance and function.
Incandescent lamp against LED on whether polarity matters, an explicit differentiation of two components.
Names the electrical circuit as the arrangement that lets electricity flow. Concept of the circuit, so LO-22 rather than LO-25, where it would be drawn.
The IEC as the body behind standard component symbols; the item belongs to the circuit-diagram convention strand.

The metal strip inside a holder makes the positive-to-negative series link, so the item turns on how the required arrangement is achieved. Not LO-17, because the strip's purpose rather than its appearance carries the answer.
